raw_response:
# Existing designs relevant to C21

Eight mechanisms are worth studying together. My design inference is to keep environment acquisition, access during invocation, and callable representation as separate decisions. No single candidate below supplies all the requested ownership, borrowing, access, and optimization guarantees.

1. **[C++ closure objects and generic call operators (N3649)](https://open-std.org/JTC1/SC22/WG21/docs/papers/2013/n3649.html).** Concrete closure classes with nonvirtual call operators provide an optimization-friendly representation and distinguish const invocation from mutable invocation. The dated 2013 paper also describes generic specialization. Its inline declaration does not guarantee machine-code inlining, and const invocation does not make captured referents immutable.

2. **[C++ generalized lambda capture (N3648)](https://open-std.org/JTC1/SC22/WG21/docs/papers/2013/n3648.html).** Per-member initialization supports explicit reference capture and moved values, offering a model for independently choosing how each environment field is acquired. This 2013 design addresses capture construction; reference lifetime checking and consuming invocation would still need separate rules.

3. **[C++ receiver reference qualification (N1821)](https://open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2005/n1821.htm).** Qualified lvalue and rvalue receivers offer a prior mechanism to distinguish read-only, mutable, and potentially consuming access to a callable environment. Applying these receiver contracts to callable objects is my inference. Rvalue qualification alone does not enforce single use. The dated 2005 introduction opened, but a detailed section fetch failed; the qualifier rules were visible in the search result.

4. **[Boost.Function 1.55.0](https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_55_0/doc/html/function/tutorial.html).** A signature-based callable wrapper with cloned targets or ref/cref targets provides an optional common dispatch interface across concrete callable types. Its tutorial was revised in 2009. This is useful for an explicit dispatch boundary; referenced targets still need lifetime discipline, and cloning does not express unique ownership.

5. **[Clang/Apple Blocks](https://releases.llvm.org/3.4/tools/clang/docs/BlockLanguageSpec.html).** Constant value captures, mutable __block cells, and explicit copying to longer-lived storage illustrate how capture behavior and escape lifetime can be separated. The [archived ABI](https://releases.llvm.org/3.4/tools/clang/docs/Block-ABI-Apple.html) supplies environment layout and cleanup hooks. [Public runtime code](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/libclosure/blob/main/runtime.cpp) provides supplementary implementation evidence, but its current version is undated here. Runtime-managed shared cells would need additional rules to express exclusive borrowing or consuming calls.

6. **[D delegates and scope closure contexts](https://dlang.org/spec/function.html).** A function/context pointer pair with allocation avoided in documented scope cases provides an alternative representation for escaping and local closures. The live specification uses garbage collection for escaping contexts. Its date is unknown, so the present scope behavior must not be treated as verified prior art at the 2014 cutoff.

7. **[GNU C nested functions in GCC 4.9.0](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-4.9.0/gcc/Nested-Functions.html).** Nested functions passed through trampolines demonstrate callbacks that directly access local variables while the enclosing activation remains alive. The [official release history](https://gcc.gnu.org/gcc-4.9/) records version 4.9.0 in April 2014, although that history page itself is later. This is a limited borrowed-callback mechanism: invoking after the captured frame ends is invalid.

8. **[Java functional-interface lambdas, JSR 335 v0.9.0](https://cr.openjdk.org/~dlsmith/jsr335/jsr335-0.9.0.html).** Targeting a callable interface while leaving object allocation and reuse flexible separates the public invocation contract from concrete closure representation. This fixed draft is marked 2013. Its final/effectively-final restriction on captured local bindings means it does not solve mutable local borrowing or ownership-consuming invocation.

For this problem, the strongest combined starting point is the concrete callable object and explicit capture construction of the C++ designs, with receiver-access contracts investigated independently. Boost.Function supplies a comparison for an optional common dispatch interface, while Blocks, D, GNU C, and Java expose different lifetime and representation tradeoffs. This is a proposed transfer of mechanisms, not evidence that the combined design was deployed or proved useful.
